lead: A spur tooth carries the whole load near its tip, like a short cantilever fixed at the root. Lewis turns that picture into one line: the root bending stress must stay below the allowable stress. Buckingham then adds the part Lewis misses — the extra load from speed, impact and tooth errors — and checks surface wear. You use these equations to choose module and face width for a gear pair in a gearbox, a machine tool, or an electric vehicle drive.
prereq: You need: bending stress and factor of safety from Unit 1, fatigue ideas from Unit 2, and the involute geometry of Chapter 7.1.

sections.h3: Lewis: the tooth as a cantilever

blocks.text: A spur tooth is a short cantilever. The tangential force Ft acts at the tooth tip — the worst case, with one tooth taking the whole load — and the root fillet is the fixed end. The bending stress at the root is highest, so the root sets the tooth size. Lewis writes the allowable tangential load as:

blocks.where: Ft is the allowable tangential load in N. σb is the allowable bending stress in N/mm². b is the face width in mm. m is the module in mm. y is the Lewis form factor, dimensionless, from tooth count and pressure angle.

blocks.text: An equivalent form is Ft = σb b π m y′, where y′ = y/π (about 0.102 when y = 0.32). Books that put π inside the formula tabulate this smaller factor; the two tabulated factors differ by the factor π. Use one form only. The right-hand side of either form is the beam strength: the load the tooth can carry at the allowable stress. It is a capacity, not the load applied by the gearbox.

For standard 20° full-depth involute teeth, y falls as the tooth count falls, because with fewer teeth the flanks are more sharply curved and the root is relatively thin (undercut below about 17 teeth), so the same load bends the tooth more. Face width is usually b = 8m to 12m. Narrower than 8m gives high bending stress. Wider than 12m does not share load evenly because of shaft deflection and misalignment.
Lewis is static. At speed, tooth errors, inertia and impact add a dynamic increment. Buckingham writes the total dynamic load Fd as:

blocks.where: Fd is the dynamic load in N. Ft is the tangential load in N. v is pitch line velocity in m/s. b is face width in mm. C is the deformation factor in N/mm², from material and tooth accuracy.

blocks.text: Two conventions exist. The AGMA/Shigley dynamic factor Kv is greater than 1: Ft,eff = Kv Ft. The velocity factor Cv in many Indian textbooks is less than 1: Ft,eff = Ft/Cv. Use one convention only; never apply both the velocity factor and the Buckingham Fd in the same check. The dynamic load is what the tooth actually feels.
Surfaces also fail by pitting. The limiting wear load is:
Fw = d1 b Q K, Q = 2z2/(z1 + z2)
blocks.where: Fw is the limiting wear load in N. d1 is the pinion pitch diameter in mm. b is face width in mm. z1 and z2 are pinion and gear tooth counts. K is the load-stress factor in N/mm², from the material pair and surface hardness.

blocks.text: Two checks close the design: Fd ≤ beam strength (σb b m y) and Fd ≤ Fw. Lewis sizing with Ft is only a first pass. Some syllabi call Fd the Buckingham dynamic load and Fw the limiting load for wear. If wear fails, raise surface hardness or size; if bending fails, raise m or b.

items: Choose z1 and z2 from the ratio. Choose a standard module m and set b = 8m to 12m.
Find pitch line velocity v = πd1n/60, with d1 = z1m. Convert d1 to metres so v is in m/s.
Find Ft = P/v, with P in watts. Use Ft to size the tooth by Lewis as a first pass: Ft ≤ σb b m y.
Compute Fd from the Buckingham equation and Fw from the wear equation.
Accept if Fd ≤ beam strength (σb b m y) and Fd ≤ Fw. Otherwise increase m, b, or surface hardness and repeat.

blocks.text: The order matters: the Lewis equation sizes the tooth, then the dynamic and wear checks test the surface and the speed effect. The worked example does only the first sizing step.

figure.caption: The flow follows the worked example: Lewis sizing gives m = 2.747 mm, the standard choice is m = 3 mm, then the dynamic and wear checks decide whether the design passes.

spec.title: Spur gear design flow
spec.aria: A flow chart runs from tooth and module choice through Lewis strength, Buckingham dynamic load and wear check to a safe or revised design.

examples.question: A 20° full-depth spur pinion has 20 teeth, allowable bending stress 120 MPa and face width 10m. It transmits 10 kW at 1200 rpm. Take the Lewis form factor y = 0.32. Find the module by Lewis sizing. This first pass takes Cv = 1.
steps: Let m be the module in mm. Pitch diameter d1 = z1m = 20m mm.
Pitch line velocity v = π(0.020m)(1200)/60 = 1.256637m m/s, with m in mm.
Lewis beam strength = σb b m y = 120 × (10m) × m × 0.32 = 384.0m² N.
Set beam strength equal to Ft: 384.0m² = 7957.75/m → m³ = 20.7233 → m = 2.747 mm.
Choose the standard module m = 3.0 mm.
examples.answer: The minimum module by Lewis is 2.747 mm, so choose m = 3.0 mm.
examples.check:
import math
P = 10000.0
n = 1200.0
v_coef = math.pi * 0.020 * n / 60.0
Ft_coef = P / v_coef
coeff = 120.0 * 10.0 * 0.32
m3 = Ft_coef / coeff
m = m3 ** (1.0/3.0)
chosen = 3.0
print(f'{v_coef:.6f}')
print(f'{Ft_coef:.2f}')
print(f'{coeff:.1f}')
print(f'{m3:.4f}')
print(f'{m:.3f}')
print(f'{chosen:.1f}')

traps: Lewis beam strength is capacity, not demand. Do not put Ft = σb b m y and call Ft the applied load; compare the applied tangential force with this capacity.
Using d1 in millimetres instead of metres inside v = πd1n/60 makes v 1000 times too large and Ft 1000 times too small. Always put d1 in metres when v must come out in m/s.
Keep m and b in mm and v in m/s. The 0.020m conversion from mm to m is a favourite place for a factor-of-1000 slip.
y and y′ are not the same: with the π inside the formula the factor is y/π, roughly a third of the other.
The final checks compare both beam strength and wear load with the dynamic load Fd; the static Ft only gives the first size.

quiz.q: State the Lewis equation for spur gear beam strength and define each symbol.
quiz.a: Ft = σb b m y, where Ft is allowable tangential load, σb is allowable bending stress, b is face width, m is module, and y is the Lewis form factor.

quiz.q: Why does the Lewis equation treat the tooth as a cantilever?
quiz.a: The tooth is fixed at the root and loaded near the tip, so the root bending stress controls strength, just like a cantilever beam.

quiz.q: A spur gear transmits 6 kW at pitch line velocity 4 m/s. Find the tangential force.
Why does increasing face width beyond about 12m not always increase load capacity?
quiz.a: Shaft deflection and misalignment stop the load from being shared evenly across the face, so the extra width does not carry its share.

quiz.q: What is the Buckingham dynamic load used for?
quiz.a: It estimates the total tooth load at speed, including the dynamic increment from tooth errors and impact, and is compared with both the beam strength and the wear load in the final checks.

quiz.q: For z1 = 20 and z2 = 60, find the wear ratio Q.
A design has Fd ≤ beam strength but Fd > Fw. What does this mean and what will you change?
quiz.a: Surface wear governs: the dynamic load is within the bending capacity but exceeds the wear load. Increase surface hardness or K, or increase size or face width, then repeat the checks.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern gear rating uses ISO 6336 or AGMA standards, which separate root stress and contact stress with many correction factors. Gear microgeometry — profile and lead corrections — reduces the dynamic increment that Buckingham lumps into one term. Finite element models now compute root fillet stress and tooth deflection directly. Search for ISO 6336 spur gear rating, AGMA 2001, and gear tooth root stress FEM.
